notes.title: Elasticsearch Implementation Plan
notes.content:
TechFlow Search — Elasticsearch Implementation Plan

Objective: Replace PostgreSQL full-text search with Elasticsearch for faster, more relevant search results.

Architecture:
- Elasticsearch cluster: AWS OpenSearch Service (2-node cluster)
- Indexing: Async via Redis + Bull queue (documents indexed on create/update/delete)
- Search API: New endpoint GET /api/search?q=term&highlight=true
- Fallback: If Elasticsearch is down, degrade to PostgreSQL FTS

Index Schema:
```json
{
  "mappings": {
    "properties": {
      "title": { "type": "text", "analyzer": "english" },
      "content": { "type": "text", "analyzer": "english" },
      "folder": { "type": "keyword" },
      "tags": { "type": "keyword" },
      "userId": { "type": "keyword" },
      "createdAt": { "type": "date" },
      "updatedAt": { "type": "date" }
    }
  }
}
```

Features:
1. Full-text search with relevance scoring (BM25)
2. Highlighted search results (matching terms bolded)
3. Filters: by folder, tag, date range
4. Fuzzy matching for typos (Levenshtein distance 2)
5. Prefix matching for instant search (type-ahead)
6. Cursor-based pagination (search_after)

Timeline:
- Sprint 21: Prototype + architecture review (DONE)
- Sprint 22: Indexing pipeline + basic query API (DONE)
- Sprint 23: Pagination, highlighting, fuzzy matching (DONE)
- Sprint 24: Launch! Feature flag rollout March 5 (THIS WEEK)

Performance Targets:
- P95 search latency: <200ms
- Indexing lag: <5 seconds (from document save to searchable)
- Zero missed documents (every doc must be indexed)

notes.title: Search API Design
notes.content:
Search API — Endpoint Design

Endpoint: GET /api/search

Query Parameters:
- q (required): Search query string
- folder (optional): Filter by folder name
- tags (optional): Comma-separated tag filter
- from (optional): Date range start (ISO 8601)
- to (optional): Date range end (ISO 8601)
- cursor (optional): Pagination cursor (from previous response)
- limit (optional): Results per page (default: 20, max: 50)
- highlight (optional): Boolean, include highlighted snippets

Response Format:
```json
{
  "results": [
    {
      "id": "doc_abc123",
      "title": "Project Alpha Notes",
      "snippet": "...working on the <mark>architecture</mark> for real-time...",
      "folder": "Work/Projects",
      "updatedAt": "2026-02-28T10:30:00Z",
      "score": 8.5
    }
  ],
  "total": 42,
  "cursor": "eyJzZWFyY2hfYWZ0ZXIiOls4LjUsImRvY19hYmMxMjMiXX0=",
  "hasMore": true
}
```

Error Handling:
- 400: Invalid query parameters
- 401: Unauthorized (missing/invalid token)
- 503: Search service unavailable (Elasticsearch down) — client should retry

Rate Limiting:
- 100 searches per minute per user
- 429 if exceeded, Retry-After header included

Security:
- Only returns documents the authenticated user owns or has access to
- User ID filter applied at query level (not post-filter)
- No cross-user data leakage possible

notes.title: Indexing Strategy & Pipeline
notes.content:
Search Indexing Pipeline — Technical Design

Architecture:
- Document events (create/update/delete) publish to Redis queue
- Bull worker processes queue, sends to Elasticsearch
- Dead-letter queue for failed indexing attempts (retry 3x, then alert)

Indexing Flow:
1. User creates/updates document → API handler saves to PostgreSQL
2. After successful DB save, publish event to 'document.index' queue
3. Bull worker picks up event:
   a. Fetch full document from PostgreSQL (ensures consistency)
   b. Transform: Extract plain text from rich content, strip HTML
   c. Index to Elasticsearch (upsert operation)
4. If indexing fails: Retry 3 times with exponential backoff (5s, 30s, 300s)
5. After 3 failures: Move to dead-letter queue, alert in #eng-alerts

Bulk Reindexing:
- For schema changes or data corruption recovery
- Script: pnpm search:reindex (processes all documents in batches of 500)
- Takes ~10 minutes for full corpus (currently ~50K documents)
- Can run in background without downtime

Consistency Guarantees:
- At-least-once indexing (may index same doc twice, idempotent)
- Eventual consistency (max 5 seconds lag)
- No index-before-persist (DB is always source of truth)

Monitoring:
- Queue depth: Alert if >100 pending jobs (indicates processing issue)
- Index lag: Alert if >10 seconds between save and searchable
- Dead-letter count: Alert on any items (should be zero)
- Elasticsearch health: Cluster status (green/yellow/red)

Cost:
- OpenSearch Service: ~$200/month (2 nodes, t3.medium.search)
- Additional Redis memory for queue: Negligible (<1MB)

notes.title: Query Optimization Experiments
notes.content:
Search Query Optimization — Experiments & Findings

Experiment 1: Analyzer Choice
- Standard analyzer vs. English analyzer
- English analyzer: Stemming (running → run), stop words removed
- Result: English analyzer produces better relevance for our content (English-only)
- Decision: Use English analyzer for title + content fields

Experiment 2: Boosting Strategy
- Title match vs. Content match weighting
- Tested: title^3, title^5, title^10
- Result: title^3 gives best user experience (title matches rise to top without overwhelming content matches)
- Decision: title^3, content^1

Experiment 3: Fuzzy Matching Configuration
- Fuzziness: AUTO vs. fixed
- AUTO: Edit distance 0 for 1-2 char terms, 1 for 3-5 chars, 2 for 6+ chars
- Result: AUTO works well, prevents false positives on short terms
- Decision: Use fuzziness: 'AUTO'

Experiment 4: Prefix Matching for Type-Ahead
- Options: match_phrase_prefix vs. completion suggester vs. edge_ngram
- match_phrase_prefix: Simple, good enough for our scale
- completion suggester: Complex setup, better for autocomplete
- edge_ngram: Best for instant results, higher storage cost
- Decision: match_phrase_prefix for MVP. Revisit at 500K+ documents.

Experiment 5: Result Freshness Bias
- Should recent documents rank higher?
- Tested: function_score with decay on updatedAt (half-life: 30 days)
- Result: Users preferred freshness-biased results for common terms
- Decision: Apply mild freshness bias (scale: 0.8, not aggressive)

notes.title: Architecture Discussion with Mike — Search
notes.content:
Architecture Discussion — Mike Torres + Tom Bradford
Date: January 28, 2026 (Architecture Review)

Context: Presenting my Elasticsearch proposal for the team search feature.

Mike's Key Feedback:

1. Circuit Breaker Pattern
- Mike: 'What happens if Elasticsearch goes down? The entire search feature breaks.'
- My response: I hadn't thought deeply about graceful degradation.
- Decision: Add circuit breaker (opossum library). After 5 failures in 30s, fall back to PostgreSQL FTS.
- This means: PostgreSQL FTS must remain functional as a backup (never remove it).

2. Dead-Letter Queue
- Mike: 'Your indexing pipeline has a single point of failure. What if Redis crashes during processing?'
- Decision: Add dead-letter queue. Failed jobs get retried 3x, then moved to DLQ with alerting.
- Implementation: Bull has built-in DLQ support. Just configure it.

3. Schema Evolution
- Mike: 'When you add new fields to the index (like tags), how do you handle existing documents?'
- Decision: Create a migration script that reindexes all documents with the new schema.
- Use index aliases so we can reindex into a new index and swap atomically.

4. Priya's Infrastructure Input
- Priya recommended: Use index aliases for zero-downtime schema changes.
- She'll set up the OpenSearch cluster and monitoring.
- Cost estimate: $200/month for 2-node cluster (approved by Alex).

My Learnings:
- Always think about failure modes. Mike's questions made my design much more robust.
- The circuit breaker pattern is something I'll use in future designs.
- Architecture reviews are valuable — even when your design is solid, fresh eyes catch blind spots.

notes.title: Elasticsearch Cluster Configuration
notes.content:
TechFlow Search — Elasticsearch Cluster Configuration

Service: AWS OpenSearch Service (Elasticsearch 7.10 compatible)

Cluster Configuration:
- Instance type: t3.medium.search (2 vCPU, 4GB RAM)
- Nodes: 2 data nodes (for redundancy)
- Storage: 50GB gp3 per node (100GB total)
- Availability zones: 2 (us-west-2a, us-west-2b)
- Dedicated master: No (not needed at our scale)

Index Configuration:
- Shards: 1 primary + 1 replica (per index)
- Refresh interval: 1 second (near real-time)
- Max result window: 10000 (for deep pagination, but we use search_after)

Security:
- Access: VPC-only (not public)
- IAM authentication for application access
- Encryption at rest (AES-256)
- TLS for data in transit
- Fine-grained access control: Application role (read/write), Admin role (full)

Backup:
- Automated snapshots: Daily at 2 AM UTC
- Retention: 14 days
- Manual snapshot: Before any schema migration

Monitoring (Priya set up):
- CloudWatch: Cluster health, CPU, memory, disk, request count
- Datadog: Custom dashboard (indexing lag, query latency, queue depth)
- Alerts: Cluster red (PagerDuty), yellow (Slack), high latency (Slack)

Cost:
- Instance: $0.064/hr × 2 = $0.128/hr ≈ $93/month
- Storage: $0.08/GB × 100GB = $8/month
- Snapshot storage: ~$2/month
- Total: ~$103/month (under Priya's $200/month estimate — good!)

Scaling Plan:
- Current: 50K documents, <100 searches/minute
- Next threshold: 500K documents or 1000 searches/minute → add 3rd node
- Future: If >1M documents, consider dedicated master nodes

notes.title: Dead-Letter Queue Implementation
notes.content:
Search Indexing — Dead-Letter Queue Design

Purpose: Handle indexing failures gracefully, prevent data loss.

Implementation:
- Library: Bull (Node.js Redis-based queue)
- Main queue: 'search.index' (processes document index requests)
- DLQ: 'search.index.dlq' (receives failed jobs after max retries)

Retry Configuration:
```typescript
const indexQueue = new Queue('search.index', {
  redis: process.env.REDIS_URL,
  defaultJobOptions: {
    attempts: 3,
    backoff: {
      type: 'exponential',
      delay: 5000  // 5s, 30s, 300s
    },
    removeOnComplete: true,
    removeOnFail: false  // Keep for DLQ processing
  }
});
```

DLQ Processing:
- Jobs that fail 3x automatically move to DLQ
- Alert fires in #eng-alerts Slack channel
- Manual intervention: Review failed job, fix issue, replay
- Admin endpoint: POST /api/admin/search/replay-dlq (replays all DLQ items)

Common Failure Reasons:
1. Elasticsearch cluster unavailable (circuit breaker kicks in)
2. Document deleted between queue publish and processing (404 from DB)
3. Malformed content causing indexing error (rare)

For case #2: Just skip (document no longer exists, nothing to index).
For case #1 and #3: Alert and investigate.

Monitoring:
- DLQ size: Should always be 0 in normal operation
- Alert: Any item in DLQ triggers Slack notification
- Dashboard: Datadog widget showing DLQ count over time

notes.title: Search Feature FAQ for the Team
notes.content:
Search Feature — FAQ for the Team
(Written by Tom Bradford)

Q: When does the search feature go live?
A: Feature flag rollout starts March 5, 2026. 10% → 50% → 100% over 3 days. Everyone should have it by March 7.

Q: What can I search for?
A: Anything in your documents — titles, content, even code blocks. Full-text search with relevance ranking.

Q: Does it search other people's documents?
A: No. You can only search YOUR documents (or documents shared with you). Privacy is enforced at the query level.

Q: How fast is it?
A: Most searches complete in under 100ms. You'll see results as you type (type-ahead with 300ms debounce).

Q: Can it handle typos?
A: Yes! Fuzzy matching is enabled. 'arcitecture' will still find 'architecture' results.

Q: What about filters?
A: You can filter by folder, tags, and date range. More filters coming in Q2.

Q: What if search is slow or broken?
A: The system automatically falls back to our basic PostgreSQL search if Elasticsearch has issues. You might notice slightly less relevant results during fallback.

Q: How fresh are the results?
A: Documents become searchable within 2-3 seconds of saving. Nearly real-time.

Q: Can I use search on mobile?
A: Yes! The search UI is responsive. Lisa designed a great mobile experience.

Q: Who built this?
A: Tom Bradford (search architecture + backend), Lisa Nakamura (frontend UI), Priya Sharma (infrastructure), Mike Torres (architecture review + mentorship).

Bugs? Questions? → #search-feature Slack channel
